Cramped words and letter spacing in NAEE

Features of interest · NAEE book links

These examples show words that can feel cramped in Taamey D even when no ink overlaps. Each family groups words that share a combination of letters and marks. A word can belong to more than one family. The families provide candidates for visual judgment rather than an exhaustive inventory of cramped words.

Each row compares the same word at usual spacing and with 0.06em extra letter spacing. The Reference opens the verse in NAEE. Current NAEE states which spacing the edition currently applies. The first three families receive automatic spacing. The two broad trial screens do not select words for automatic spacing.

Counts cover Scripture in NAEE, including ketiv and qere. Counts distinguish different spellings and pointing, including accent marks; occurrences count each appearance. Notes and words with special letter or vowel formatting are excluded. Adding the family totals would double-count words that belong to more than one family.

  1. A broad vowel and accent on a narrow letter
  2. Shapes where Taamey D adds spacing
  3. A raised vowel on yod before qof
  4. Adjacent narrow letters, both with below-marks
  5. Qof and its predecessor, both with below-marks

A broad vowel and accent on a narrow letter

In this family of words, yod or vav carries both a broad below-vowel and a below-accent. The vowel dots and accent share a narrow letter’s space. This family is expanded automatically in NAEE.

Shapes where Taamey D adds spacing

In this family of words, Taamey D adds space in particular combinations of narrow letters and below-marks, near final descending letters, and where a hataf vowel precedes an accented narrow letter. NAEE gives these words its additional spacing as well. These examples show the six observed shapes selected from the font’s spacing rules.

A raised vowel on yod before qof

In this family of words, Taamey D raises yod’s vowel to make room beside the following qof’s vowel and below-accent. NAEE adds horizontal space to separate the neighboring groups of marks more clearly.

Adjacent narrow letters, both with below-marks

In this family of words, two adjacent narrow letters each carry below-marks. Broad vowel dots or an extra below-mark leave less room between the sets of marks. These examples include vav beside yod and nun beside vav. This broad screen remains a trial; a matching word can receive automatic spacing from a more specific family.

Qof and its predecessor, both with below-marks

In this family of words, qof and the letter immediately before it in reading order both carry below-marks. Qof’s descending stroke adds to the crowding around those marks. The examples include broad vowel dots on the predecessor, an extra below-accent on qof, and an extra below-accent on the predecessor. This broad screen also remains a trial; a matching word can receive automatic spacing from a more specific family.
